initial_plan.can_answer: yes: the file has a reported pedestrian-killed count per crash, so its annual totals can answer the question as recorded in this dataset
initial_plan.metric: annual sum of number_of_pedestrians_killed across crashes
initial_plan.denominator: none; a count of reported pedestrian deaths, not a rate
initial_plan.population: all police-reported NYC motor vehicle crash records dated 2013-01-01 through 2025-12-31
filters: crash_date is in calendar years 2013 through 2025

data_check.findings: The selected population contains 2,132,218 crash rows across 2013–2025. Every year has coverage from January 1 through December 31. No selected row has a missing crash date/year or a missing number_of_pedestrians_killed value. January 1 dates occur 188–485 times per year and do not form a dominant/default-date pileup relative to annual row counts. Annual crash-row counts vary from 231,564 in 2018 to 85,546 in 2025.
data_check.decision: Keep all rows in the selected years; no rows are excluded or reclassified. The outcome field is present for all selected rows, and each requested year has full calendar-date coverage.

final_plan.can_answer: yes, as recorded in this dataset; the dataset cannot independently verify completeness of police reporting
final_plan.metric: For each calendar year, the sum of number_of_pedestrians_killed across all included crash records; each field value is the reported number of pedestrian deaths for that crash
final_plan.denominator: none; annual count of reported pedestrian deaths, not a rate
final_plan.population: All police-reported NYC motor vehicle crash records with crash_date in calendar years 2013–2025 inclusive
final_plan.years: Calendar years 2013 through 2025 inclusive; every year is fully covered by dates in the file
final_plan.limitations: The total is limited to police-reported crashes and reported pedestrian-killed counts; full date coverage does not establish complete reporting. Annual crash-row counts vary substantially (231,564 in 2018 versus 85,546 in 2025), so annual totals are counts rather than exposure-adjusted rates and should not be read as rates of risk. The check found zero missing outcome values among the included rows.
